title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how artificial intelligence has been researched and applied in higher education, and what this body of work reveals for educators. The authors note that AI in education has expanded rapidly, but that educators often lack clarity about how AI can be used pedagogically, what kinds of applications dominate the literature, and whether researchers adequately address ethical, pedagogical, and institutional risks. The review therefore asks how AI in higher education has been conceptualised, what types of studies and publication patterns exist, what application areas are most common, and to what extent ethical implications are discussed.

The study uses a systematic review methodology. The authors searched EBSCO Education Source, Web of Science, and Scopus for peer-reviewed journal articles in English or Spanish, initially identifying 2,656 records and ultimately including 146 empirical primary studies published between 2007 and 2018. The reviewed studies focused on AI applications in higher education only. The synthesis groups AI applications into four main categories: profiling and prediction; assessment and evaluation; adaptive systems and personalisation; and intelligent tutoring systems. Across these categories, the review describes uses such as predicting student dropout or admission, automated grading and feedback, personalised course recommendations, academic advising, learner modelling, and tutoring systems that support content learning, feedback, or collaboration.

The population and context are higher education settings, especially undergraduate students, with a smaller number of studies focused on postgraduate students and many studies not specifying level. The review also highlights the roles of educators and administrators because some AI systems were teacher-facing or system-facing, such as tools for course evaluation, academic advising, retention monitoring, and institutional decision support. Most first authors came from computer science or STEM rather than education, and most empirical studies used quantitative methods. Geographically, the literature was dominated by work from the United States, China, Taiwan, and Turkey.

The main conclusions are that AI research in higher education is growing, but is heavily shaped by technical disciplines and quantitative methods, with relatively little leadership from educators. The literature emphasizes operational and instructional efficiencies—especially prediction, assessment, personalisation, and tutoring—but shows weak engagement with pedagogical theory and almost no sustained critical reflection on ethics, privacy, or broader risks. The authors conclude that future work should better connect AI applications to educational theory and should more seriously examine ethical and educational challenges, rather than focusing mainly on technical performance and feasibility.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with explicit search, screening, and coding procedures over 146 studies, which strengthens credibility. However, it is not a meta-analysis, does not synthesize pooled causal effects, and covers heterogeneous mostly quantitative but not uniformly high-causal-quality studies, so it falls below blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broadly promising but heterogeneous and mostly indirect impacts, especially for operational efficiency and some learning outcomes in higher education. Because effects are not pooled, many findings are descriptive or accuracy-based rather than standardized educational impacts, and relevance to K-12 literacy is adjacent rather than direct, overall impact is best rated as unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI applications in higher education that prominently includes machine-learning-based profiling and prediction for admissions, dropout/retention risk, student modeling, and early identification of low-engaged or at-risk students.
Review covers AI-based assessment and evaluation tools such as automated grading, automated essay scoring, and feedback generation on student work, including writing-related feedback systems.
Review synthesizes adaptive systems and personalization tools that tailor content, pacing, recommendations, and learning pathways based on student profiles or learner models.
Review includes classical intelligent tutoring systems used to teach course content, diagnose knowledge gaps, provide hints/feedback, curate materials, and sometimes facilitate collaboration.
Review includes language-learning and writing-focused AI applications such as automated essay scoring, lexical-feedback tools, and second-language learning systems.
Review notes intelligent virtual reality and simulation-based environments where virtual agents support authentic or game-based learning experiences.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education literature, AI systems for automated grading, prediction, and tutoring were consistently framed as improving efficiency by reducing instructor or administrative workload, speeding assessment, and enabling support at scale. Specific examples cited in the review include automated essay scoring with 94.6%-98.2% agreement with human raters in one medical-education study and prediction systems with high classification accuracy, but the review does not report a pooled effect size across the 146 included papers.
finding.measure: Agreement with human raters, classification accuracy, workload reduction, time/cost savings described across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial institutional uptake of AI for admissions, retention, advising, and management functions, with many studies reporting accurate prediction of dropout, admissions, and engagement; for example, machine-learning models in reviewed studies often outperformed logistic regression, and one dropout model achieved 81.19% accuracy. At the same time, the authors conclude that the field shows almost no critical reflection on ethical risks, privacy, pedagogy, and educator roles, indicating meaningful institutional promise alongside governance and implementation concerns.
finding.measure: Institutional prediction accuracy, administrative use cases, and narrative synthesis of ethical/governance concerns across the review corpus

finding.finding_summary: The review includes adjacent postsecondary evidence on AI writing and language tools, such as automated essay scoring and writing-feedback systems, suggesting these tools can score essays with high agreement to human raters and may encourage revision. However, the review also notes persistent concerns about feedback quality, genre suitability, and whether such systems benefit beginning language learners, with no pooled literacy effect size reported.
finding.measure: Essay scores, agreement with human raters, revision behavior, quality of writing feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across reviewed higher-education studies, intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems generally showed positive or satisfactory preliminary results for learning in domains such as computer science, business statistics, accounting, and medicine. The review cites prior meta-analytic evidence that ITS had a moderate effect on student learning and outperformed many non-human instructional methods, though they were less effective than human tutoring; no new pooled effect estimate is calculated in this review.
finding.measure: Course learning outcomes across higher-education subjects; narrative synthesis of included studies
finding.effect_size: moderate effect referenced from prior meta-analysis, exact value not_reported in this paper

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies student engagement and motivation as measurable outcomes in adjacent AI-in-higher-education studies, including engagement prediction from VLE data and modeling of academic motivation. Findings suggest AI can detect low engagement and support intervention planning, but the paper does not provide pooled evidence that AI directly improves motivation or engagement outcomes, and some adaptive/dialogue systems showed weaker results in delayed post-tests.
finding.measure: Student engagement indicators, motivation models, VLE clickstream/behavioral data, delayed post-tests in selected adaptive system studies
